# Identifying the Emission Control Tube on a Yamaha XS400

When you inherit a classic bike like a 1979 Yamaha XS400, the engine bay often holds clues to decades of regulatory changes that didn't always come with an instruction manual. You are looking at a dual-carburetor setup, likely Mikuni VM24s or similar units common on that era's parallel-twin engines. The tube protruding from one carb while the other is capped isn't a fuel line or an accidental breach; it is a deliberate modification mandated by emissions legislation.

This component is an evaporative emission control (EVAP) vent line, specifically tied to the charcoal canister system. In modern vehicles, this is often integrated seamlessly under the seat or into the tank assembly, but on older European-market bikes from the late 70s, the physical routing was sometimes left exposed or modified during initial compliance testing. The primary function of this tube is to manage fuel vapor pressure within the carburetor bowls and the fuel tank.

### How the System Works

Carburetors operate by creating a vacuum in their float bowls to meter fuel into the engine. However, as gasoline evaporatesâespecially in hot climates or during prolonged idlingâit creates significant internal pressure. Without relief, this pressure can force liquid fuel up through the vent port (the small hole usually visible on top of the carburetor body) and out into the air filter or intake manifold.

This is where the tube comes in. It connects the carburetor vent to a charcoal canister located elsewhere on the frame or under the seat. The canister acts as a reservoir, trapping fuel vapors until the engine is running and creating a vacuum at the throttle body. At that point, the stored vapors are drawn into the intake manifold to be burned along with the air-fuel mixture.

The fact that one tube is active and the other is capped confirms this is a system-specific requirement rather than a generic feature on every carburetor. On many US-spec models of the XS400, both carbs might have had ports plugged or routed differently because the emission standards were less stringent or the testing methodology varied by region. The cap you see on the second carb indicates that specific port was never intended to be active in your particular configuration.

### Implementation Considerations for Restoration

If you are prepping to remove the engine, handling this tube requires care beyond just disconnecting it. Before removing the bike from the stand, you must trace the routing of this active tube. In many cases found on XS400s, these lines were originally routed through a flexible hose that connected to a canister hidden beneath the seat or near the rear shock mounts.

If the original path is damaged or missing, attempting to guess the route will fail. The trade-off here is between simplicity and compliance. Leaving the tube open to the atmosphere (by capping both ends) causes fuel starvation at high RPMs because the vacuum created in the bowl pulls fuel directly into the filter. Conversely, installing a generic canister from a modern car may not fit the geometry of a 1979 frame without significant fabrication.

The most robust approach for a restoration is to locate the original canister mounting point. If the canister itself has degraded (charcoal media turns to dust over time), you can replace just the unit while retaining the original routing hardware. This maintains the correct pressure dynamics that the carburetor tuning relies upon. Tuners often adjust the idle mixture screw based on the assumption that the vacuum system is functioning correctly; a blocked or misrouted vent line will throw off these adjustments, leading to a rough idle or hesitation under load.

### Why the Second Port Was Blocked

The presence of a capped port on the second carburetor highlights a critical detail about emissions compliance: it was not a universal requirement for all bikes of that year, but a specific fix for certain markets. Regulators often required that only one carburetor bowl be vented to the canister to limit the total volume of vapors entering the emission control system, or simply because the testing equipment only monitored one side.

Attempting to connect both tubes to a single canister without verifying the flow characteristics could introduce backpressure issues. The original engineering decision was likely to balance the vacuum draw across the two carbs, ensuring that neither bowl became starved of fuel while maintaining adequate vapor recovery. Disregarding this asymmetry and trying to make it symmetrical is a common pitfall for DIY restorers who prioritize aesthetics over functional mechanics.

If you decide to reinstall the engine, verify that the active tube leads directly to a sealed canister with fresh charcoal media. Do not leave it open to the atmosphere, even temporarily, as this will alter the fuel delivery characteristics immediately upon starting the engine.
